lawyer:
M. Quamrul Haque Siddique with AKM Alamgir Parvez, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner.
Rokanuddin Mahmud with Syed Mamun Mahbub, Advocates ----- For Respondent No. 1.
M. Khaled Ahmed with Md Ashiqur Rahman, Advocates -----For Respondent No.7.
parties:
Jamal Uddin (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Major General Abdus Salam (Retired) and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Khurshid Alam Sarkar J: This Rule has been issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the holding of the Office of the Member of Parliament (MP) from the constituency No. 154 Mymensingh-9 (Nandail) by respondent No. 1, as declared by the Election Commission, shall not be declared to have been held without lawful authority and of no legal effect and, further, to show cause as to why respondents No.2 and 4 shall not be directed to declare the seat of the Member of Parliament from the constituency No. 154 Mymensingh-9 (Nandail) held by respondent No. 1 vacant and thereby hold fresh election for the said seat with- in 90 days from the date of decision, and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Succinctly, the facts of the case, as stated in the writ petition and supplementary affidavit, are that the petitioner, by virtue of being an inhabitant of Village- Tashra, Upazilla-Nandail, District-Mymensingh, is a constituent of constituency No. 154, Mymensigh-9 (Nandail) wherefrom Major General (retired) Abdus Salam (hereinafter referred to as respondent No. 1) has been elected in the 9th parliamentary election and since then holding the post of Member of Parliament (MP). In the estimation and consideration of the petitioner, respondent No. 1 is a disqualified person to be elected and, thereby, to hold the public office of MP, as per provisions of our Constitution and Representation of the People's Order, 1972, and, as such, the petitioner has brought this application under Article 102(b)(ii).

3. It is stated that on 23-11-2008 respondent No.1 submitted his nomination paper as a candidate of 9th parliamentary election for the constituency No. 154, Mymensingh-9 (Nandail) and on 4-12-2008 the same was cancelled by the Returning Officer (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.9) on the ground of being a 'loan defaulter' and when an appeal was preferred by respondent No.1, the Election Commission (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.3) dismissed it on 10-12-2008.

4. Side by side, on 4-12-2008 respondent No. 1 filed the writ petition No. 9819 of 2008 (hereinafter referred to as 'other writ petition') challenging the legality and propriety of the action of Bangladesh Bank and others in inclusion of his name in the CIB report as a 'loan 'defaulter' and the same was though moved before this Court but was adjourned for 11-12-2008. Then, by filing a supplementary-affidavit as to the cancellation of his nomination paper, respondent No.1 prayed for giving a direction upon respondent No. 9 and respondent No.3 to accept his nomination paper and an interim order of direction was passed upon the said respondents to allow respondent No. 1 to contest in the aforesaid election albeit no Rule was issued on the orders cancelling the nomination of respondent No. 1 passed by the Election Commission and Returning Officer. Thereafter, when the 'other writ petition' was placed before a Division Bench of the High Court Division on 17-12-2008, the said interim order of direction dated 11-12-2008 was extended till disposal of the Rule. It is stated that respondent No.1, after obtaining the aforesaid favourable order from this Court, did never bother to take any step to get the 'other writ petition' heard. Having been won in the 9th parliamentary election, respondent No.1 took oath as a Member of Parliament and since then he has been holding the post of MP. It is stated that since respondent No. 1 did never challenge the legality of the orders of cancellation of his nomination paper either in this Court nor in Election Tribunal and, as such, orders passed by the Returning Officer on 4-12-2008 cancelling his nomination paper and the order passed by the Election Commission on 10-12-2008 affirming the Returning Officer's said order dated 4-12-2008 are still in operation and their findings of fact, on the CIB report published by the Bangladesh Bank that respondent No. 1 is a 'loan defaulter', do stand correct. It is stated that since the petitioner was a 'loan defaulter', he was not and, even, at present is not legally eligible and competent to be a Member of Parliament and to hold the said post. Therefore, having been aggrieved by the holding of the position of MP by respondent No.1, the petitioner seeks to challenge the authority of respondent No. 1 to the post of MP. Hence, this Rule.

5. While respondent No. 1 contested the case by filing affidavit-in-opposition, supplementary affidavit and placing relevant laws, references and arguments and respondent NO.7 (Janata Bank Ltd) opted to appear in the instant case by filing Vokalatnama only, the remaining respondents namely, Bangladesh Jatio Shangshad (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.2), Bangladesh Election Commission (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.3), Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.4), Credit Information Bureau of Bangladesh Bank (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.5), Dynamic Textile Industries Limited (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.8) and the Deputy Commissioner, and the Returning Officer, Mymensingh (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.9) did not avail of the opportunity of appearing before this Court.

6. Respondent No. 1 by filing affidavit-in- opposition contends, inter alia, that he participated in the 9th national parliamentary election as a valid candidate in pursuant to the order dated 11- 12-2008 passed by a vacation Bench of this Hon'ble Court in 'other writ petition' and was elected for the constituency No. 154, Mymensingh- 9 legally. It is stated that one Mr Advocate Abdul Hai was a nomination aspirant from Bangladesh Awami League and was willing to be a MP candidate from the same constituency but Awami League had nominated respondent No. 1 and having been unsuccessful in getting nomination from the party, he started to perturb respondent No.1, first time, by issuing a legal notice through his Advocate-on- Record on 14-12-2008 threatening that a Civil Miscellaneous Petition for Leave to Appeal is being awaited to be moved against the interim order dated 11-12-2008 passed by the vacation Bench of the High Court Division allowing respondent No. 1 to contest in the 9th parliamentary election and, now, it is the same person who, in disguise, have employed the present petitioner to file the instant writ petition after nearly 4 and half years.

7. Mr Quamrul Haque Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, at the very outset places Article 66(2)(g) of our Constitution, section 27ক of the Bank Company Act, 1991 and various articles of the Representation of the People Order (RPO), 1972 (hereinafter referred to as RPO) and submits that articles 12(1)(1) and 12(1)(m) of the RPO mandates that if an individual or a director of a company defaults in repaying any loan, then he shall be disqualified to be a candidate for parliamentary election. He then submits that the aforesaid disqualification continues to operate even after being elected as a Member of Parliament in view of the words used therein and, as such, holding of the post of the Member of Parliament by a 'loan defaulter' is completely illegal. He submits that respondent No. 1 was found to be a 'loan defaulter' by the Returning Officer as well as by the Election Commission and these findings of facts have never been overturned by any Court of law or by any authority, nor respondent No. 1 himself has been able to prove that he was not a 'loan defaulter'. He submits that respondent No. 1 has already withdrawn the 'other writ petition' and, as such, the orders passed by the Returning Officer on 4-12-2008 remains in operation.

8. He submits that the claim of respondent No.1 as to having resigned from the post of directorship of respondent No.8-company has not been approved by the concerned bank as required by section 27 K of the Bank Company Act, 1991 and, as such, the claimed resignation of respondent No. 1 is not a resignation in the eye of law and, therefore, he was, at the time of submission of his nomination paper as a candidate for 9th parliamentary election, a 'loan defaulter' and continues to be the same till date.

9. He submits that the manner of presentation of 'other writ petition' by respondent No.1 before this Court is capricious, misleading and designed to secure an order from this Court by practising fraud in that the said writ petition was filed challenging the CIB report only, but an interim order in the form of a direction was obtained from this Court enabling the petitioner of the said 'other writ petition' to contest in the election and, subsequently, the period of aforesaid interim order was obtained till disposal of the said Rule though no challenge was made against the propriety of the order of cancellation of his nomination paper by the Returning Officer and by the Election Commission. He submits that with the adjudication upon of the said Rule, the disqualification or incompetency of the present respondent No. 1 to become an MP shall never be removed.

10. Mr Siddique continues to submit that respondent No. 1 challenged the legality of the rejection order of his nomination only recently during the hearing of the matter but, according to him, issuance of the said Rule cannot also shield him to remain as an MP inasmuch as it has been settled by a series of decisions of our Apex Court that no writ lies against an order passed by the Returning Officer or the Election Commission regarding any election matter. He submits that when this Hon'ble Court ordered to analogously hear and dispose of the 'other writ petition' and the instant writ petition, respondent No. 1 withdrew the aforesaid 'other writ petition' amid hearing of the Rules having found the position of law against him. He submits that after withdrawing the aforesaid case, the order passed by the Returning Officer, Mymensingh on 4-12-2008 stands valid and, thereby, it has now been an admitted position that respondent No. 1 was a 'loan defaulter' at the time of filing his nomination paper and the same position still continues in the light of the fact that respondent No. 1 has not been able to prove his position that he repaid the said loan or he has duly and lawfully resigned from the post of director of respondent No. 8- Dynamic Textile Industry Limited.

11. In a bid to deal with the allegation of lacking bonafides in approaching this Court, as raised by respondent No. 1 in his affidavit-in-opposition against the petitioner, Mr Siddique submits that the petitioner is a local leader of Awami league in addition to being a voter of the constituency wherefrom respondent No. 1 has been elected as a Member of Parliament and, thus, he has every right to see that the MP of his constituency must not be a person disqualified in the eye of law. He submits that if the other person's grievance, including Mr Advocate Abdul Hai's who is stated to be the rival candidate of respondent No.1, appears to echo the petitioner's, it does not necessarily mean that the petitioner's standing will be questionable, rather it helps in strengthening and substantiating the claim that the grievance is of public nature.

12. He prays to this Court that there should be a direction upon respondent No.1 to refund the salaries, privileges and incentives taken by him. He submits that this sort of direction now has been the demand of time to set up an instance for the usurpers of public offices that illegal holding of public office ends up with serious consequences.

13. In reply to a query, as to the extent of jurisdiction of this Court in dealing with the quo warranto matters, he submits that this Court should not confine itself within the four corners of the words employed in Article 1 02(2)(b )(ii) as it simply empowers this Court to issue a show cause notice upon the usurper of a public office. He cites the maxim "Ibi jus ubiremedium" and submits that there must be a remedy against a wrong and in view of the fact that the framers of the Constitution have imposed the duty of issuing a show cause notice to the usurper, thus, by implication it means that this Court has also been endowed with the power of making any order; including any consequential relief, otherwise, incorporation of Article 1 02(2)(b )(ii) in the Constitution is rendered meaningless. He places the form, style and manner of the prayers made in the instant writ petition and submits that in order to overcome any question which may likely arise that since it is a writ of quo warranto, declaration as to unseating respondent No. 1 is beyond the jurisdiction of this Court, prayer in the form of certiorari in tandem with seeking a mandamus has also been made.

14. In support of the above submissions Mr Siddique refers to the cases of (1) AFM Shah Alam vs Mujibul Huq reported in 41 DLR (AD) 68, (2) Mahmudul Haque (Md) vs Md Hedayetullah reported in 48 DLR (AD) 128, (3) AKM Mayeedul Islam vs Bangladesh Election Commission reported in 48 DLR (AD) 208, (4) Dr Mohiuddin Khan Alamgir vs Government of the People s Republic of Bangladesh reported in 62 DLR (AD) 425, (5) University of Mysore vs Govind Raa AIR 1965 SC 491 (6) Lt. Col. Farzand Ali vs Province of West Pakistan 22 DLR (SC) 203 and (7) Abu Bakar Siddique vs Justice Shahbuddin Ahmed reported in 49 DLR 1. By making the aforesaid submissions, the learned advocate for the petitioner prays for making the Rule absolute.

15. Mr Khaled Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for respondent No.7 (Janata Bank Ltd), adopts the submissions of Mr Siddique and begs apology for not filing a separate affidavit for the instant writ petition as he was under an impression that since both the writ petitions were ordered to be heard analogously and the subject matter of both the cases being the same, filing one affidavit in any of these cases would suffice to establish the fact that respondent No.1 was and still is a 'loan defaulter'. Thereafter, with the permission of this Court he refers to annexures-D, E & F to the 'other writ petition' and annexure-Xl to the affidavit-in-opposition of the said writ petition and submits that respondent No.1 is a shareholder of respondent No.8, a public limited company, and when the said company took a loan of Taka nine crore from respondent No.7, he furnished a personal guarantee to secure the said loan. He submits that respondent No.8-company till date has not repaid the loans for which a suit in Artha Rin Adalat is pending. He submits that until the loan of the bank is repaid, respondent No.1 remains a 'loan defaulter' irrespective of the fact whether he has resigned from the post of directorship of the said company.

16. Per contra, Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Advocate appearing for respondent No.1, at the very outset of his submission places Article 66(4) of our Constitution and submits that since respondent No.1, having been a 'Returned Candidate' in the 9th parliamentary election, is now performing his functions as a Member of Parliament and as per the provisions of our Constitution, the dispute should be raised in Parliament and the Hon'ble Speaker will refer the matter to the Election Commission and, then, the latter will give the final decision as to whether respondent No. 1 should hold the position and continue to function as a Member of Parliament.

17. He then submits that in whatever manner respondent No. 1 has been elected in the 9th parliamentary election, at present, the defacto position is that he is an elected MP and, therefore, after being elected as a Member of Parliament there are two forums to challenge his election or holding of his position as a Member of Parliament. If, Mr Mahmud continues to submit, there is an allegation as to the election dispute, then a contesting party could have taken the matter before the Election Tribunal but in the case of respondent No. 1 there was no such allegation by any contesting person in the election of respondent No. 1 and the other forum, available for the petitioner or any other aggrieved person to raise a complain as to the disqualification of respondent No. 1, is Parliament. He submits that as per section 3 of the Members of Parliament (Determination of Disputes) Act, 1980 the disputes of present nature can easily be sent to Parliament by sending a letter to the Speaker who then will be in a position to refer the matter to the Election Commission for its decision and by not doing so the petitioner has chosen the wrong forum and, therefore, he submits that the present writ petition is a misconceived one and not maintainable.

18. He submits that the 'other writ petition' was rightly filed to challenge the action of the Bangladesh Bank in inclusion of the name of respondent No. 1 in the CIB list as well as the orders of the Election Commission and the Returning Officer who had cancelled the nomination paper of respondent No.1 on the ground of being a 'loan defaulter' in the light of the fact that respondent No.1 had never held more than 25% of allotted shares as required to be a 'loan defaulter' under the Proviso of section 5(গগ) of the Bank Company Act 1991 and, furthermore, he resigned from the post of director well before of the 9th parliamentary election and pursuant to filing the said writ petition this Court rightly directed the Election Commission and the Returning Officer to accept the nomination paper of respondent No. 1 and, as such, Mr Mahmud submits that there was no illegality by the High Court Division in entertaining the said writ petition and, thereby, in contesting the 9th parliamentary election by respondent No. 1 inasmuch as there was no other alternative forum for seeking redress given that the Election Tribunal was not in existence at that relevant point in time and, further, in Election Tribunal only the 'contesting candidate' is entitled to agitate any election dispute meaning that under the said law, an individual candidate who contested the election can file case against another con- testing candidate for adjudication upon the matters relating to cancellation of election result, vote counting, rigging and other election related disputes but a person, like the present respondent No. 1, whose nomination paper has been cancelled by the Returning Officer, being not a 'contesting candidate', cannot go to Tribunal for vindication of his legal right.

19. Mr Mahmud submits that there was nothing to get from 'other writ petition' after respondent No. 1 was allowed to contest the 9th parliamentary election and, further, since the CIB report also does not show his name therein any longer, it would have been a futile exercise to continue with the said 'other writ petition'. Mr Mahmud further submits that the said writ petition was filed challenging the decision of the Returning Officer and the Election Commission basing on the CIB report but in view of the fact that the Election Commission and the Returning Officer themselves declared respondent No. 1 a valid 'Returned Candidate' in the 9th parliamentary election, their previous orders dated 10-12-2008 and 4-12-2008 stood revoked and, accordingly, they refrained from appearing in both these writ petition, otherwise, their actions will amount to 'approbation and reprobation' if they now again claim their initial orders as to cancellation of nomination paper to be correct.

20. Mr Mahmud submits that without, at first, challenging the actions of the Election Com- mission in publishing the Gazette Notification by declaring respondent No. 1 as an elected MP, the instant writ petition in the form of quo warranto is not maintainable and, he adds that, in order to impugne the said Gazette Notification an application under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) is to be brought where the petitioner will be required to satisfy the Court that he is a 'person aggrieved'.

21. He also submits that in order to be competent as a writ petitioner in a writ of quo warranto, the petitioner is required to establish the fact that he has approached this Court bona fide but since it transpires from the chronology of events of this case that Advocate Abdul Hai earlier had tried to file a Civil Miscellaneous Petition for Leave to Appeal in the Appellate Division against the High Court Division's direction dated 11-12- 2008 to resist respondent No. 1 from contesting the 9th parliamentary election and having been unsuccessful in his earlier attempt, now, he is conspiring to oust respondent No. 1 from the position of MP by filing this writ petition with an ulterior motive to keep him away from the upcoming to" parliamentary election, the present writ petition fails on this account alone.

22. He finally submits that issuance of a writ in the quo warranto proceedings is completely a discretionary power of this Hon'ble Court and the said power has been used in UK, USA and in this sub-continent very sparingly. A writ is generally issued in our jurisdiction only when the Court has been satisfied that law of the land has not created any forum for vindication of the wrong claimed of; that it finds the alleged wrong to be a public grievance, not a private grievance; that the petitioner is challenging the holding of a Constitutional office/public office; that the Court is satisfied about the bona fides of the petitioner in approaching this Court and also satisfied that there has been a 'clear violation' of any Constitutional or statutory provisions in appointing or holding the said public office but, in the case at hand, there being no such 'clear violation' of any law and the remedy sought for by the petitioner being beyond the jurisdiction of Article 102 (2)(b)(ii), the writ should be recalled and, thereby, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

23. Mr Rokonuddin Mahmud, to substantiate his submission, relies on the following case laws of our jurisdiction and the same of abroad; (1) Panjab Land Development &Reclamation Corporation Ltd vs Presiding Officer, Labour Court (1990) 3 SCC 682, (2) Mamleswar vs Kanhaiya AIR 1975 (SC) 907, (3) Nilkantha vs Manmohan(1975) CLJ 404, (4) Daud vs Bangladesh reported in 17 BLC (HCD) 506, (5) Abdur Rob Miah vs District Registrar and others reported in 4 BLC (AD) 8, (6) Dr Kamal Hossain vs Mohammad Sirajul Islam reported in 21 DLR (SC) 23 and (7) Shaikh (Md) Obaidullah Raihan vs Sayed Shahidul Haque Jamal, reported in 54 DLR 280.

24. We have heard the learned advocates for both the sides, perused the writ petition, affidavit- in-opposition, supplementary affidavit with their annexures and the relevant laws and decisions placed before us and have considered them very carefully.

25. It appears that, subject to the satisfaction about the technical issues raised herein including the maintainability of this writ petition, the core issue for adjudication upon by this Court is whether respondent No.1 was a 'loan defaulter' within the purview of the provisions of article 12(1)(1) and 12(1)(m) of the RPO and, further, whether Article 66(4) of the Constitution debars the petitioner to challenge the alleged disqualification of respondent No. 1 to approach this Court.

26. Since the question of maintainability of this writ petition has been raised on the ground of non-invocation of other equally efficacious forum on top of levelling the allegation of lacking bona fides against the petitioner, this Court is required to deal with the said technical issues at first. However, we prefer at first to embark upon the task of examination of the substantial issue with an aim to provide with a better understanding on the factual and legal analysis of the case as a whole.

27. Accordingly, let us first see whether respondent No. 1 is a 'loan defaulter' or not. In order to adjudicate upon the said issue we are to know about the financial relationship of respondent No. 1 with respondent No. 7-Janata Bank Limited and respondent No.8-company and for that purpose we have to take recourse to the affidavits and statements made in the 'other writ petition' and the annexures appended therewith. It is worthy to note here that the said writ petition and the instant writ petition were listed for analogous hearing by this Court but in course of hearing the said Rules, 'other writ petition' was discharged on 3-10-2013 on the prayer of the learned Advocate for the petitioner thereto (herein respondent No.1) on the ground of being infructuous as it was submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner of the said writ petition that after giving a direction upon the Election Commission to allow the petitioner of the said writ petition to contest in the 9th parliamentary election, he virtually obtained his aspired remedy. Since both these writ petitions were taken up for analogous hearing and though the Rule issued in 'other writ petition' has been adjudicated upon a bit earlier in point of time by discharging the same, we can validly take judicial notice of and profitably rely on the statements, affidavits made in the said writ petition and affidavits-in-opposition and examine the annexures appended thereto.

28. It is the admitted position of respondent No.1 of this writ petition, as appears from annexures-D, E and F to 'other writ petition' that he was a shareholder and a director of respondent No.8- Dynamic Textiles Industry Limited and when the said company availed of a loan facility of Taka 9 (nine) crore, respondent No.1 furnished a personal bank guarantee, as appears from annexure- X1 to the 'other writ petition'. But the case of respondent No. 1 is that since he has never held more than 25% of the allotted shares and already resigned from the post of directorship before the election and, accordingly, as per the Proviso of section 5 (গগ), he is not a 'loan defaulter'. Now, let us vet the position of respondent No. 1 within the purview of section 5(গগ) which reads as follows:

“খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা” অর্থ কোন ব্যক্তি বা প্রতিষ্ঠান যাহার নিজের বা স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠানের অনুক’লে প্রতদ্দ অগ্রীম, ঋণ বা উহার অংশ বা উহার উপর অর্জিত সুদ বাংলাদেশ ব্যাংক কর্তৃক জারীকৃত সংজ্ঞা অনুযায়ী মেয়াদোত্তীর্ণ হওয়ার ৬ (ছয়) মাস অতিবাহিত হইয়াছেঃ

তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা কোন পাবলিক লিমিটেড কোম্পানীর পরিচালক না হইলে অথবা উক্ত কোম্পানীতে তাহার বা উহার শেয়ারের অংশ ২৫% এর অধিক না হইলে, উক্ত পাবলিক লিমিটেড কোম্পানী স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান বলিয়া গন্য হইবে নাঃ

আরো শর্ত থাকে যে, পাবলিক লিমিটেড কোম্পানী ব্যতীত অন্য কোন প্রতিষ্ঠানে ঋণ গ্রহীতার শেয়ারের অংশ অনধিক ২০% হইতে উক্ত প্রতিষ্ঠান এই দফার অধীন স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে না।

29. It is an admitted position that respondent No.8-company is a public limited company and respondent No. 1 is a director of the said company and, therefore, the first part of the Proviso “.......খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা কোন পাবলিক লিমিটেড কোম্পানীর পরিচালক না হইলে..........” clearly attracts the position of respondent No.1. His plea that he has resigned from the post of the director appears to be untrue from the statements made by respondent NO.7 Janata bank in 'other writ petition' which may be quoted herein below.

Writ petitioner's resignation as a Director of respondent No.6 has never been accepted by the Board of Directors of the concerned Bank. Therefore, his resignation is not effective within the meaning of 27(ka) of the Banking Companies Act, 1991 and, as such, writ petitioner is a defaulter and his name was included in the list of CIB in accordance with law.

30. Section 27 ক of the Bank Company Act, 1991 reads as follows:

দেনাদার কোম্পানীর পরিচালকের উপর বিধি-নিষেদ। আপাততঃ বলবৎ অন্য কোন আইনে যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন, ঋণদাতা ব্যাংক বা আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানের (ঋণ বা বিনিয়োগ অনুমোদন কারী কর্তৃপক্ষের একস্তর উর্দ্ধতন কর্তৃপক্ষের) অনুমোদন ব্যাতীত কোন দেনাদার কোম্পানীর কোন পরিচালকের পদত্যাগ কার্যকর হইবেনা এবং কোন পরিচালক তাঁহার শেয়ার হস্তান্তর বা বিক্রয় করিতে পারিবেন না।

31. It is vividly apparent from the above pro- visions of law that the resignation of any director of a loanee-company shall not be effective until the loan provider-bank approves it. Since the Bank confirms that it has not accepted the resignation of respondent No.1, we find that respondent No. 1 remains to be a director of the loanee company-respondent No. 8 against whom Artharin case is pending for recovery of defaulted payment of the bank and that is how respondent No.1 is a খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা within the ambit of section 5(গগ) of the Bank Company Act, 1991. What is more that had the initial Rule of 'other writ petition' even been made absolute by declaring the inclusion of his name in the CIB report illegal, it could not save respondent No. 1 from being disqualified as a MP given that a loanee may still remain a 'loan defaulter' even without being included his name in the CIB list until the loan provider-bank does not raise any claim against him. However, the Rule in the said writ petition has been discharged on 3-10-2013 and, thus, it appears that with the discharging of the said Rule issued in 'other writ petition', the disqualification or incompetency of respondent No.1 has not been removed or does not get cured, rather, the orders passed by the Election Commission and the Returning Officer get their lives back inasmuch as those were stayed for a period till disposal of the said Rule issued in 'other writ petition'. There was no challenge against the legality of the orders passed by the Election Commission and the Returning Officer by respondent No. 1 until the issue was raised by this Court in the midst of hearing of the said 'other writ petition'. The above scenario has been depicted in our judgment and order dated 3-10-2013 passed in discharging the 'other writ petition', which is reproduced herein below:

This writ petition has a very interesting chequered history because the writ petition was filed by the petitioner challenging the inclusion of the name of the petitioner in the CIB report prepared and published by Bangladesh Bank and sent to respondent No. 5 (the Returning Officer) treating the petitioner as a defaulter in payment of bank loan. But the petitioner did not challenge the cancellation of the nomination paper by respondent No.5 nor did he challenge the dismissal order of appeal by the Election Commission filed by the petitioner against the cancellation of nomination paper. Interestingly, after filing of the writ petition on 4-12-2008 the same was made stand over till 11-12-2008 when the petitioner filed supplementary affidavit narrating the facts of cancellation of the nomination paper by the Returning Officer and dismissal of the appeal by the Election Commission. In the supplementary affidavit the petitioner did not pray for amendment of the prayer as to challenging the cancellation of nomination paper. However, on the self same prayer as made in the writ petition, a vacation Bench sitting singly passed an order in the following terms:

"Pending hearing of the substantive application, respondent Nos. 5 and 7 are directed to accept the nomination paper of the petitioner in respect of constituency No. 154, Mymensigh-9 for the parliamentary polls scheduled to be held on 29th December, 2008".

Furthermore, it appears from the record that another supplementary affidavit has been filed by the petitioner annexing the copy of the dismissal order of appeal by the Election Commission and thereafter when the matter was placed before a regular bench the Rule was issued in the following terms:

"Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents No.I-5 to show cause as to why the insertion or inclusion of the name of the petitioner in the CIB report prepared and published by respondent No. 1 and sent to respondent No. 5 treating the petitioner as defaulter in payment of bank loan shall not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect and or such or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

Let the interim order dated 11-12-2008 passed by the vacation bench shall remain in force till disposal of the Rule."

So, it appears that without challenging and praying for any-remedy as to the cancellation of the nomination paper and dismissal of appeal by the Election Commission the petitioner got a relief by an order of this Court through the vacation Bench and thereafter he was elected and has been holding the post of Member of Parliament (MP) till date. Subsequently, on 19-6-2013 the petitioner filed an application for issuance of supplementary Rule and upon hearing, supplementary Rule was issued in the following terms:

"Let a supplementary Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 10-12-2008 dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the order dated 4-12-2008 passed by respondent No.5 cancelling the nomination paper of the petitioner submitted for contesting the 9th parliamentary election from constituency No. 154, Mymensingh-9 shall not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and of no legal effect".

Today, when the item is taken up for hearing, Mr Rokanduddin Mahmud, the learned Counsel, submits that since the petitioner has already been elected in the election held on 29-12-2008 and he has already completed his term and, as such, with the passage of term, the Rule has become infructuous leaving nothing for adjudication by this Court. Under such circumstances, the Rule is discharged for being infructuous.

However, there will be no order as to cost.

32. This Court though had intended to adjudicate upon the Rule in the said 'other writ petition' on merit upon dealing with all the issues raised therein, including the question as to whether the petitioner in the said Rule is a 'loan defaulter', whether inclusion of his name in the CIB list was legal and whether this Court has jurisdiction to entertain a matter relating to or arising out of election, however, on the prayer of the learned Advocate for the petitioner of the said writ petition, the, Rule was discharged only on the ground of being in fractuous with a summary judgment and order. Our particular interest was to hover on and carry out a scrutiny as to whether a person whose nomination has been cancelled by the Returning Officer and Election Commission being not a contesting candidate as per the provision of RPO can approach this Court as this Court was inquisitive to examine the words 'no election ... to Parliament shall be called in question except by an election petition' employed in Article 125(b) of our Constitution. No definition or meaning of 'election petition' has been provided in our Constitution. However, section 2(ix) of the RPO provides that an 'election petition' means a petition under article 49 of the RPO and the article 49 allows only a 'candidate' as defined in article 2(ii) of the RPO to present, an election petition and, thereby, to see whether the judgments passed by our Apex Court in the cases of AFM Shah Alam vs Mujibul Huq, 41 DLR (AD) 68, Mahmudul Haque vs Md Hedayetullah, 48 DLR (AD) 128, AKM Mayeedul Islam vs Bangladesh Election Commission, 48 DLR (AD) 208, Dr Mohiuddin Khan, Alamgir vs Government of the People s Republic of Bangladesh 62 DLR (AD) 425 rendered per in curiam in adjudication upon the cases at hand. Among all the afore cited cases, AFM Shah Alam vs Mujibul Huq is the pioneer and all the above cases have followed the ratio decidendi of the AFM Shah Alam's Case. The fundamental difference between the fact of the said case is that in AFM Shah Alam's Case nearly two thousand 'contested candidates', who were unsuccessful in the union parishad election, challenged the role and function of the Election Commission but in the instant cases, where an aspirant candidate's nomination is cancelled by the Returning Officer and upon an appeal the cancellation order is affirmed by the appellate authority, the question arises whether this Court should decline its power under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) for such like persons.

33. In our scrutiny and judgment, we did not find any reason not to interfere with the decision passed by the appellate authority, the same being a final decision, under Article 14(5) of the RPO, Rule 15(1) of স্থানীয় সরকার (সিটি কর্পোরেশন) নির্বাচন বিধিমালা, 2010,Rule 15(1) of স্থানীয় সরকার  (পৌরসভা) নির্বাচন বিধিমালা, 2010,Section 18(1) of স্থানীয় সরকার (উপজেলা পরিষদ) নির্বাচন বিধিমালা, ২০১০, and section 15(1) of স্থানীয় সরকার (ইউনিয়ন পরিষদ) নির্বাচন বিধিমালা, ২০১০, if it clearly suffers from malice-in-Law or corum-non-judice and the relief sought by the petitioner may be granted without disturbing the election schedule because completion of election process being a Constitutional obligation of a Constitutional body must not be protracted on the basis of a grievance of an individual candidate. In entertaining the aforesaid grievance, this Court must be satisfied at first before issuing any Rule as to whether there is any apparent illegality in the impugned order passed by the Returning Officer and the appellate authority. The Court must com- ply with the provisions of Article 125(c) of our Constitution which provides that no Court shall pass any interim order without hearing the Election Commission.

34. In order to mitigate this kind of situation, the office of the Election Commission may correspond with the office of the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh requesting the latter to assign one or two Division Bench entrusted with the power of dealing with election matters only just before the election commences so that the lawyers and officers of the Election Commission may constantly be present in the Court rooms and assist this Court to handle those petitions expeditiously. Upon hearing both the parties if the Court is satisfied to issue Rule with a direction upon the concerned authority to accept the nomination paper of a candidate, in that event, the Election Commission must take necessary initiatives to get the Rule heard within shortest possible time, preferably within a span of 2-3 months, by the said Rule issuing Bench. The Election Commission should not allow an alleged disqualified candidate to hold the post of MP by virtue of an interim order of the Court for a long period. When the Election Commission will demonstrate a serious attitude that a 'loan defaulter' or otherwise incompetent candidate might succeed to con- test in the Election and be a 'Returned Candidate' capitalising the interim order of the Court, how- ever, his tenure may soon come to end by disposing of the Rule, the confidence of the 'loan defaulters' class will be demoralised and thereby may abstain from abusing the process of the Court. Having been deprived of getting the opportunity to examine the said issues on this occasion, we may await to have a judgment from our Apex Court in a fit case covering the above points in the time to come.

35. Be that as it may, for the purpose of adjudication upon the case at hand, we have already found that respondent No. 1 is a loan defaulter' under section 5(MM) of the Bank Company Act, 1991. In addition to that, he is also a 'loan defaulter' under articles 12 (1)(L) and 12 (1)(m) of the RPO, which read as follows:

12(1). Any elector of a constituency may propose or second for election to that constituency, the name of any person qualified to be a member under clause (1) of Article 66 of the Constitution.

Provided that a person shall be disqualified for election as or for being a member, if he-

(a) ..........................................................................

(b) ..........................................................................

(c) ..........................................................................

(d) ..........................................................................

(e) ..........................................................................

(f) ..........................................................................

(g) ..........................................................................

(h) ..........................................................................				.

(i) ..........................................................................

G) ..........................................................................

(k) ..........................................................................

(I). being a loanee, other than who has taken small loan for agricultural purposes, has defaulted in repaying before 1 [fifteen days] from the day of submission of nomination paper any loan or an installment thereof taken by him from a bank or financial institution;

(m). is a director of a company or a partner of a firm who has defaulted in repaying before 2[fifteen days] from the day of sub-mission of nomination paper any loan or an installment thereof taken by him from a bank or financial institution;

36. In view of the fact that respondent No. 1 has not been released from his personal guarantee furnished by him in favour of the bank for securing the loan of respondent No.8-company, we find him to be disqualified for election, and to remain, as an MP under article 12(1)(1) of RPO, 1972. We also find him to be disqualified for election, and to perform function, as an MP under article 12(1)(m) of RPO, 1972 as we have already found that he remains a director of respondent No. 8-company.

37. After adjudication upon the afore discussed moot question by dealing with the same comprehensively, we may now turn to take up all the technical issues pertaining to the question of maintainability of the instant writ petition on the count of non-availing of other forum and lacking bona fides in bringing the instant petition as well as the power of this Court as to the extent of granting relief under Article 1 02(2)(b )(ii).

38. The apparent forums for adjudication upon this kind of case are; (i) an application under Article 102 (2)(a)(ii) and 102(2)(b )(ii) which have been chosen by the petitioner for the instant writ petition (ii) notifying the Speaker with a request to refer the dispute to the Election Commission as suggested by Mr Mahmud (iii) filing a case before the Election Tribunal and (iv) approaching the civil Court in discourse of the case. Among all the technical issues, we may first take up the question of availability of alternative legal forum and thereafter the question of bona fides would be examined.

39. In order to properly adjudicate upon the said issue, at first this Court requires to have a good grasp on Articles 102(2)(b)(ii) and 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution, under which the instant application has been filed. The said Articles read as follows:

(2) The High Court Division may, if satisfied that no other equally efficacious remedy is provided by law................

(a) on the application of any person aggrieved. make an order-(ii)declaring that any act done or proceeding taken by a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority has been done or taken without lawful authority and is of no legal effect; or

(b) on the application of any person, make an order-(ii) requiring a person holding or purporting to hold a public office to show under what authority he claims to hold that office.

(underlined by us)

40. A careful reading of the said Articles provide a two stage scrutiny, namely (i) this Court, at first, is to undertake a task of examination as to whether the law of the land has created any forum for dealing with the matter and, only then, (ii) a duty on this Court is cast as to detecting and considering the violation of any law by any person in holding a public office.

41. It appears that the petitioner has invoked the 'Special Original Jurisdiction' of this Court, apparently, under Article 102(2)(b)(ii) and also under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of our Constitution. Jurisdiction under Article 102(2), as a whole, is known as extraordinary jurisdiction and the same is to be availed of only when there is 'no other equally efficacious remedy' available. The framers of the Constitution have intended that the people at first must search for and approach an appropriate legal forum other than the Constitutional Court. It is only then the Constitutional Court should be availed of when the citizen will find that the state has not created any legal forum for them for the aspired remedy. Thereafter, subject to the 'satisfaction' of this Court, a writ petition may be entertained. Article 102(2) of our Constitution may be quoted in this context. 'The High Court Division may, if satisfied that no other equally efficacious remedy is provided in law ..... .'. It appears from the words employed in' the said Article that 'if satisfied' strongly suggests that this 'Special original jurisdiction' of the High Court Division may be invoked only upon the satisfaction of the High Court Division as to the non-availability of the 'other equally efficacious remedy' (underlined for emphasize), In our view, the scrutiny as to the competency of invoking this 'Special original jurisdiction' is required to be made by this Court before issuance of any Rule, not by issuing of any Rule in view of the clear and unambiguous words of our Constitution 'if satisfied'. Now, the question as to whether 'other equally efficacious remedy' is available for obtaining a declaration concerning an illegal holding of a public office, such as the present case at hand, requires a minute examination.

42. Mr Mahmud submits that forum under Article 66(4) of our Constitution is the appropriate forum for adjudication upon the issue raised in this case and attacks this writ petition to be not maintainable as the subject matter of this case is beyond the jurisdiction of this Court in view of the provisions of the said Article 66(4) of the Constitution. For ease of reference and under- standing let us cite the said Article which reads as follows:

66(4) If any dispute arises as to whether a member of Parliament has, after his election. become subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in clause (2) or as to whether a member of Parliament should vacate his seat pursuant to article 70, the dispute shall be referred to the Election Commission to hear and determine it and the decision of the Commission on such reference shall be final.

43. It is the cardinal principle of Constitutional interpretation that Constitution should be read and understood by attributing ordinary meaning. From a lucid reading of the said Article it is understable without any difficulties that the disqualification referred to therein is one which occurs 'after his election', not a pre-existing one. There cannot be a second meaning of the said Article inasmuch as we do not find any ambiguities in discerning the words engraved in our Constitution both in English and Bengali version.

44. In the case at hand the disqualification mentioned in Clause (2) of Article 66 was levelled against respondent No. 1 before the election in that the loan was taken by him as a director of respondent No.8-company before the election and the bank itself (respondent No.7) claimed that respondent No.1 was a 'loan defaulter' and, as of now, his position remains unchanged as the company has failed to repay the loan or he could not release his personal guarantee furnished at the time of securing the loan facilities in favour of respondent No.8-company. If the claim of the bank would have been raised only after respondent No.1 became elected as an MP, Article 66(4) would have been attracted. So, our unhesitant conclusion is that the disqualification of respondent No.1 is a pre-election one, which surfaced at the time of election and, thus, forum under Article 66(4) of our Constitution is not the forum for adjudication upon the issue agitated in this case.

45. The second type of forum is Election Tribunal. Let us look at the relevant laws of the land governing the election case.

Article 125(b) of our Constitution: no election to the [office of President] or to Parliament shall be called in Question except by an election petition presented to such authority and in such manner as may be provided for by or under any law made by Parliament.

Relevant provisions of RPO read as follows:

2(vi). "contesting candidate" means a candidate who has been validly nominated for election as a member and has not withdrawn his candidate;

2(ix). "election petition" means an election petition made under Article 49;

49.(1) No election shall be called in question except by an election petition presented by a candidate for that election in accordance with the provisions of this Chapter.

(2) An election petition shall be presented to the High Court Division within such time as may be prescribed.

Rule 33 of জাতীয় সংসদ নির্বাচন পরিচালনা বিধিমালা, ২০০৮: নির্বাচনী দরখাস্তঃ অনুচ্ছেদ ১৯ বা অনুচ্ছেদ ৩৯ এর অধীন নির্বাচিত প্রার্থীর নাম সরকারী গেজেট প্রকাশিত হইবার পঁয়তাল্লিশ দিনের মধ্যে সংক্ষুদ্ধ পক্ষ সুপ্রীম কোর্টেও হাইকোর্ট বিভাবে নির্বাচনী দরখাস্ত পেশ করিতে পারিবে।

46. From the concurrent reading of the said provisions of the Constitution, statute and Rule, it is crystal clear that in order to qualify to be a petitioner in the Election Tribunal, the petitioner must be a person who had contested in the election and the subject matters of the "election petition" have also been enunciated therein.

47. Question, thus, comes up for consideration very pertinently as to whether the said dispute, being raised at the time of election by the Returning Officer, does fall within the definition of 'election dispute' as provided in RPO, 1972 and, therefore, the matter should be adjudicated upon by the Election Tribunal. Apparently, though the sum and substances of the case of the petitioner, regardless of his prayer under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) or 102(2)(b)(ii), is to declare the election of respondent No.1 illegal, the petitioner being not a 'contesting candidate' could not have taken the matter to the election Tribunal as per the said provisions of Article 125(b) of our Constitution, articles 2(vi), 2(ix), 49 of the RPO, 1972 and Rule 33 of নির্বাচনী আচরন বিধিমালা। Thus, we hold that the present petitioner was not a con- testing candidate and, as such, he is not allowed by law to go to Election Tribunal. Our view is supported by the ratio decidendi of the case of Lt. Col Farzand Ali vs Province of Pakistan 22 DLR (SC) 203 wherein it was held that-

I can see no reason why relief by way of quo warranto should not be available in a case where the remedy by way of an election petition is no longer possible or it is not the appropriate remedy or the disqualification is a continuing one which debars a person not only from being elected to an office but also from holding that office.

48. Now, the third type of forum is civil Court. Let us see whether jurisdiction of our civil Courts may be appropriate for dealing with the matter inasmuch as section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure confers jurisdiction upon the civil Courts to try all suits of civil nature by using the word 'shall' therein. Section 9 reads as follows;

Section 9. Courts to try all civil suits unless barred.- The Courts shall (subject to the provisions herein contained) have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred.

Explanation-A suit in which the right to property or to an office is contested is a suit of a civil nature, notwithstanding that such right may depend entirely on the decision of questions as to religious rites or ceremonies.

49. From the ratio decidendi of innumerable Stare Decisis of this sub-continent such as (i) Dildar Ahmed vs Farroque Ahmed, 27 DLR (AD) 138, (ii) BN Khan Degree College vs Abdur Rahim, 7 BLT (AD) 153, (iii) Satish Chandra vs Dharanidhar, AIR 1940 (iv) Sinha Ramanigh vs Ranga Rananaja, AIR 1961 SC 1720 (v) Lutfar Rahman vs Waliur Rahman, AIR 1943 Cat. 59 (vi) LIC of India vsIndia Automobiles, AIR 1991 SC 884 (vii) Secretary of State vs Mark, AIR 1940 PC 105 (viii) Illuri vs Ap, AIR 1964 SC 322 (ix) Gurbux Singh vs Financial Commr, AIR 1991 SC 435 (x) Solaimari Bibi vs Administrator 45 DLR 727 (xi) Md Shahidullah vs Abdus Sohan, 1996 BLD 423 = 49 DLR 248 (xii) Kamrul Ahsan vs Ziauddin, 11 BLT 63 (xiii) Dwaraka Prasad vs Ramesh Chandra AIR 2003 SC 2696 (xiv) Shamsuddin vs Shamsuzzaman 22 DLR 655 (xv) Deputy Secretary vs Nizamuddin Haider, 1985 BLD 57 = 37 DLR 102, it is apparent that when any person is aggrieved by an act done or proceedings/decision taken by a private individual or by a statutory body or by a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority, he may seek a declaration from the civil Courts. Since resorting to the civil Courts is relatively easier and convenient for any person, in terms of pecuniary expenses, communication and time, for its location being available in each of the District of our country, it is to be considered as a 'better forum' provided in law and, thus, calling it an 'equal forum' is a striking understatement. From our experience of sitting in Writ Bench, we have noticed that the learned members of the Bar place the argument that approaching the lower Courts is not efficacious as it cannot pass any interim order against the Government or statutory bodies without first hearing them. In reply to the said argument our observation is that until a petitioner in his petition makes out his case that he, on an urgent basis, desperately needs an interim order immediately, only then there may be a scope to concede to the aforesaid argument subject to the verification that he has rushed to this Constitutional Court immediately and he did not squander any time negligently in approaching this Court. Thus, we find that our civil Courts are better forum than the High Court Division for adjudication upon any matter related to declaration of a legal right or for establishment of a claim as to violation of any law excepting enforcement of any fundamental right.

50. Although our view is that our civil Courts are empowered to issue a show cause notice upon a holder of a public office asking him to show cause as to how he is holding the office, however, in view of the fact that the petitioner might encounter difficulties to overcome the issue of his standing as a plaintiff and, particularly, when in most of the common law countries, including ours one, Constitutional Court has been resorted to for dealing with the cases of alleged illegal usurpation of any public office, such as the present one, without ever being questioned by our Apex court, we are of the view that choosing the High Court Division by the petitioner as the forum for dealing with and adjudication upon this kind of matter appears to be justified, for, the same being in consonance with the provisions of our Constitution as well as the practice and convention of the common law countries. Thus, we hold that forum under Article 66(4) of our Constitution or the Election Tribunal or the civil Court are not capable of providing 'equally efficacious remedy' to the petitioner and, therefore, the forum under Article 102(2) of the Constitution is the appropriate one.

51. Now the technical issue whether In a quo warranto proceedings this Court is empowered to make any order to declare that the holder of the public office is holding the alleged office illegally and is liable to be ousted from the said office and respondent No. 1 should be directed to refund to the exchequer the remunerations and other pecuniary privileges taken as an MP and, further, whether the Election commission be directed to arrange for re-election for the said constituency, in other words, whether the relief can be granted up to the extent as made in the prayer or this Court should refrain from making any order other than mere recording the information received from the respondents as to the authority under which respondent No. 1 is holding the post.

52. On the whole our simple and plain under- standing on the Constitutional wordings of Article 102(2)(b)(ii) cited hereinbefore, in tandem with the submissions of both the sides, is that our Constitution has vested this Court with the power of asking a person who is holding or purporting to hold a public office to explain his position as to whether he is holding the said post legally or not and, accordingly, this Court's power appears to be limited up to the extent of issuing show cause notice upon the alleged usurper of the public office and after receiving the information from the said usurper of public office, the task of this Court is to examine as to whether he has been placed or appointed by a lawful authority, whether he has requisite qualification for holding the said post and whether the procedure for the said placement/appointment was followed, in other words, whether the relevant provisions of the law of the land have been complied with in placing/appointing the alleged public office holder. Our Constitution, however, does not endow this Court with the power of passing any consequential order as prayed for by the petitioner to oust respondent No. 1 from his office or to direct the Election Commission to arrange for re-election given that we do not find any ambiguity in the wordings of the Constitution in this regard. However, on the strength of the words used therein 'The High Court Division may make an order', we are of the view that this Court's power is not confined only within issuing show cause notice but also to 'make an order' in the form of declaration as to whether respondent No. 1 is holding the post of MP lawfully or not. We opined that granting any consequential relief is beyond the scope of Article 1 02(2)(b )(ii) which may amount to addition or importation of some words therein causing amendment of the Constitution tanamounting to transgression of an exclusive jurisdiction of Parliament. Mr Qumrul Islam Siddique has endeavoured to link the case of University of Mysore vs Govinda Rao AIR (SC) 491 (relevant Para 7) on this particular point to substantiate his submission that this Court is empowered to grant consequential relief. However, in our way of scrutiny of the relevant Para 7 of the cited case we find that it is a quotation of Halsbury and from its minute reading it transpires that 'the usurper can be ousted' by the order of this Court and by conceding to his argument up to that extent in line with the wordings of our Constitution 'to make an order' this Court is inclined, in adjudication upon this case, to declare that respondent No. 1 is an usurper to the office of Member of Parliament.

53. This Court generally provides ancillary relief in the application made under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of our Constitution but it is apparent from the 'cause title' as well as prayer of the instant writ petition that no decision or action of the Government or Election Commission or any other local authority has been challenged in this writ petition. The petitioner has the option to challenge the election notification of respondent No. 1 in the form of certiorari under Article l02(2)(a) (ii) upon satisfying this Court that he is a 'person aggrieved' as a constituent of the constituency in question and this Court usually grants ancillary and consequential reliefs in addition to making a declaration as to the legality or propriety of the said notification, Since the present writ petition is not in the form of certiorari, then, it becomes pertinent to see whether this Court is competent enough to take up the task of examinations which require for adjudication upon the issues raised, here, in this quo warranto proceeding.

54. In the case of State of Haryana vs Harayana Co-operative Transport Ltd, AIR 1977 (SC) 237, wherein challenging alongside the validity of an award given in favour of two labours by the Judge of a Labour Court, the eligibility of the Judge to hold the office of a Judge also was challenged and the Indian Supreme Court held that a petitioner of certiorari application, in the same application, also has the standing to make prayer for the relief usually sought in a Quo warranto proceeding. Accordingly, if we con- sider the intent of the writ petition, which is to challenge the 'election of respondent No. 1 as an MP and thereby holding of the said post', then there will be no difficulty to remedy the petitioner. In the case of Abu Baker Siddique vs Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed 49 DLR 1 where an Advocate of this Court Mr Abu Baker Siddique challenged the appointment of the former Chief Justice Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed in the post of the President of the Republic of Bangladesh on the ground of 'disabilities of the judges after their retirement' as prescribed in Article 99 of our Constitution. The cause title was drafted in the form of a quo warranto application though the challenge was actually against the appointment notification for the said post and when an objection was raised that since Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed was yet to take oath for the said office and, as such, he not being the holder of the post, quo warranto proceeding does not lie, the Court on its own volition transformed the quo warranto petition into a certiorari application after substantiating the locus standi of Advocate Abu Baker Siddique on the following reasonings:

"There may be some wrong mentioning of the Article in the cause title of the application and there may be some misconceived prayer in the prayer portion of the writ petition, yet the spirit, substance and necessary intent of the writ petition is to be gathered from reading the writ petition as a whole"

<u>55. However, the ratio decidendi of the cited Indian case is not applicable in the present case given that it was a certiorari petition where his locus standi was already approved by the Court as a "person aggrieved" and a "person aggrieved" may also convert his position into 'any person' as required for becoming a petitioner in a writ of quo warranto proceeding. However, a petitioner of a quo warranto proceeding being "any person" requires to convert himself into an 'aggrieved person' for which his standing is to be established as was done in the afore cited case of Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed. In the light of the fact that the petitioner has not portrayed himself as a 'person aggrieved' and this Court also finds it difficult to carry out an exercise as was done by the Court in the case of Chief Justice Shahbuddin, thus, in this case we do not find any scope to convert the present quo warranto proceeding into the certiorari for the reason that the petitioner is not an 'aggrieved person' but 'any person'.</u>

<u>56. As to the issue whether the impugned post is a public portfolio, no dispute has been raised from the side of the respondents. Admittedly, the post under challenge is a public office in the light of the fact that the office of an MP and his title is substantive in nature and he is independent in discharging his duty and the procedure for removal of the Members of Parliament from their respective offices is not same to that of a government servant. As to the issue of the nature of the grievance i.e. whether it is to be taken as a public grievance, we find that the subject matter of the writ petition comes within the purview of 'common concern' of the commoners in that the post of Member of Parliament, whose primary duty is to legislate the law, should not be portrayed to the general people that a law maker is holding the said portfolio by violating the law.</u>

57. So far as the objection taken by the respondents on the petitioner's intention in filing the instant writ petition, we do not find any element of mala fide that can be leveled against the petitioner inasmuch as the petitioner being a voter of the constituency of respondent No. 1 has every legitimate right to see that the MP of his constituency is not holding the said post illegally. The allegation raised against the petitioner that he has been engaged by the rival local Awami league leader, Advocate Abdul Hai, can hardly stand in the way of filing. the instant writ petition inasmuch as filing of this type of writ petition by Mr Advocate Abdul Hai himself would not have been mala fide given that the post in question being of a public nature, petitioner's intention appears to be of secondary importance and, thus, the ratio decidendi of the cases of Dr Kamal Hossain vs Mohammad Sirajul Islam 21 DLR (SC) 23 and Abdur Rob Miah vs District Registrar 4 BLC(AD) 8 is not applicable here in this case.

58. Accordingly, upon being satisfied that there is no other equally efficacious forum and having been found the petitioner's present move to be bona fide, we hold that the instant writ petition is maintainable and declare that respondent No.1 was a disqualified person and remains to be the same to be a Member of Parliament.

<u>59. After such declaration made by this Court that respondent No.1 is a disqualified person to perform function as a Member of Parliament, the provisions laid down in Article 66(4) shall come in to operation and, accordingly, the office of the Hon'ble Speaker may be notified about the outcome of this case.</u>

60. We though do not fancy to grant any consequential relief in the form of directing respondent No. 1 to refund the remuneration and other privileges taken by him from the State as an MP, such as enjoyment of duty free car, government accommodation and other facilities, for the reasons discussed hereinbefore, however, we opine that this is a fit case where exemplary costs should be extracted from respondent No. 1. The rationale behind our aforesaid view is that our threadbare examination as to the intention and purpose of filing the 'other writ petition', coupled with the style and manner of dealing with the same by respondent No.1, leads us to believe that though it was known to him that he was a 'loan defaulter' and was disqualified to contest in the election and thereafter to remain as an MP, somehow in an unusual manner he managed to contest the election on the strength of a weird interim order of this Court. Furthermore, he was not willing to have the matter heard after getting the interim order extended on 14-12-2008 till disposal of the Rule as evident from the record that no step was taken for fixing the Rule in any Court until this Court ordered to bring the matter in the list and, even thereafter, the hearing was made delayed initially on the ground of filing supplementary affidavit and, later, on different occasions on the plea of the personal difficulties of the Senior Counsel.

<u>61. It is, thus, apparent that respondent No.1 had the intention to abuse the process of this Court in getting an interim order and, thereby, to enable him to contest in the election and, thereafter, to continue in the post of MP without disposing of the Rule. What is more striking that in none of the writ petitions (the other writ petition and the present one) respondent No. 1 has come up with any assertion that the defaulted loan has been paid. The very purpose of the enactment of this piece of legislation was to put the 'loan defaulter' class away from election but if the said 'loan defaulter' people get chance to contest in the election by abusing the process of the Court, the legislation is rendered nugatory. The above conducts of respondent No.1 deserves to be answered by slapping a cost of high volume and, thereby, disseminating the message to the citizens of the country that consequence of filing a frivolous litigation with an aim to achieve any favourable order by abusing the process of this Court is fatal.</u>

62. Accordingly, respondent No.1 is directed to pay a cost of Taka ten lakh in favour of the exchequer by way of treasury challan.

63. In the result, the Rule is made absolute in part.

The office is directed to send a copy of this judgment to the Office of the Hon'ble Speaker and another copy to the Office of Election Commission for their information and necessary actions.

End.
